history.heading: Māori settlement
paragraphs: New Zealand (Aotearoa in Māori) was one of the last major landmasses settled by humans. Polynesian voyagers arrived from East Polynesia around 1250–1300 CE, becoming the Māori people. They developed a distinctive culture organised into iwi (tribes) and hapū (sub-tribes), and hunted the giant flightless moa to extinction.
Dutch navigator Abel Tasman sighted the islands in 1642, and James Cook mapped them in 1769–70.

history.heading: Treaty of Waitangi and colonisation
paragraphs: European whalers, traders and missionaries arrived in the early 19th century. In 1840 the British Crown and many Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi, New Zealand's founding document; differences between the English and Māori texts over sovereignty have been debated ever since.

British settlement grew rapidly, and the New Zealand Wars (1845–1872) were fought over land and sovereignty. Large areas of Māori land were confiscated or sold, and the Māori population declined sharply before recovering in the 20th century.

history.heading: A pioneering nation
paragraphs: In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote. It built an early welfare state and became a dominion in 1907. New Zealand soldiers fought at Gallipoli in 1915, commemorated on Anzac Day.

From the 1970s, a Māori cultural revival led to the Waitangi Tribunal, which investigates breaches of the treaty, and settlements returning land and resources. Economic reforms in the 1980s liberalised the economy. New Zealand declared itself nuclear-free in 1987. In 2019 a terrorist attack on two mosques in Christchurch killed 51 people, leading to gun law reforms.

culture.heading: Bicultural identity
paragraphs: English, Māori (te reo Māori) and New Zealand Sign Language are official languages. About 17 percent of people identify as Māori, and there are large Pacific Islander and Asian communities. Christianity is the largest religion, but nearly half of New Zealanders report no religion.

Māori culture is central to national identity: the haka (a ceremonial dance), the hangi (earth oven), carving and tattooing (tā moko). New Zealanders call themselves "Kiwis" after the native flightless bird.

culture.heading: Sport and the outdoors
paragraphs: Rugby union is the national sport, and the All Blacks are one of the most successful teams in history, performing the haka before matches. Sailing, netball and cricket are also popular. Dramatic landscapes, used as the setting for The Lord of the Rings films, make the outdoors central to life.

politics.heading: Parliamentary democracy
paragraphs: New Zealand is a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy with the British monarch represented by a governor-general. It has no single written constitution. The unicameral parliament is elected by mixed-member proportional representation, with seats reserved for Māori. The main parties are the centre-right National Party and centre-left Labour Party.
Treaty of Waitangi issues and Māori rights are prominent political debates. New Zealand is a leader in Pacific affairs and a member of the Five Eyes intelligence alliance.

economy.heading: Agriculture and tourism
paragraphs: New Zealand has a developed, market economy heavily based on agriculture. It is the world's largest exporter of dairy products (through Fonterra) and a major exporter of meat, wool, kiwifruit, wine and timber. China is the largest trading partner.

Tourism, international education and film production are important. Most electricity comes from renewable sources, mainly hydro and geothermal. The currency is the New Zealand dollar. Challenges include housing affordability and productivity.
